decks.title: Chemical Changes and Reactions — Part 1: Direct combination and decomposition
goals: Identify direct combination reactions and write balanced equations for examples
Write balanced equations for decomposition by heat, light and electricity
Describe the observations that go with each reaction

slides.heading: Joining and splitting
slides.body_md: Part 1 — in a **direct combination** two substances join; in a **decomposition** one substance splits. Each is a different kind of chemical change.

visual.alt: Flow: A and B combine to give AB, which can decompose again into A and B

slides.narration: Chemical changes can be sorted by what happens to the substances. Sometimes two substances join to make one new substance. Sometimes one substance splits up into simpler ones. We start with joining and then look at splitting.

slides.heading: Direct combination
slides.body_md: In a **direct combination** reaction two or more substances unite to form **one** product.

rows: Red glow; black solid that a magnet does not attract

visual.alt: Table of four direct combination reactions with conditions and observations

slides.narration: In a direct combination, the reactants unite to give a single product. Heated iron and sulphur glow red and make a black solid which a magnet cannot pick up. Magnesium burns with a dazzling white flame and leaves white ash.

slides.heading: Equations for direct combination

visual.alt: Table of five balanced equations for direct combination reactions

slides.narration: Here are balanced equations for five direct combinations. Notice that the number of atoms of each kind is the same on both sides. In the last one, an electric spark makes nitrogen and oxygen of the air join to form nitrogen monoxide.

slides.heading: Compounds can combine too
slides.body_md: The reactants need not be elements. A **compound** can combine with another compound or element to give one product.

visual.alt: Calcium oxide plus water gives calcium hydroxide
visual.caption: Quicklime and water: much heat is given out.

slides.narration: Quicklime joins with water to form slaked lime. The mixture hisses, turns hot and may give off steam. Another example is ammonia gas meeting hydrogen chloride gas, which gives dense white fumes of ammonium chloride.

slides.heading: Quick check: direct combination
slides.body_md: Look at the number of products.

visual.alt: Zinc plus sulphur gives zinc sulphide

slides.narration: Zinc powder and sulphur are heated and form zinc sulphide. Which kind of reaction is this?

slides.heading: Decomposition
slides.body_md: In a **decomposition** reaction one compound splits into two or more simpler substances. Energy is needed: **heat**, **light** or **electricity**.

visual.alt: Flow from decomposition to heat, light and electricity

slides.narration: Decomposition is the opposite of combination. One compound is split into simpler substances. It never happens without energy, which may come as heat, as light, or as an electric current.

slides.heading: Decomposition by heat

rows: Green powder turns black; gas turns lime water milky
White solid; residue yellow when hot, white when cold
Brown fumes; residue yellow when hot, white when cold
Gas that relights a glowing splint

visual.alt: Table of four thermal decomposition reactions with products and observations

slides.narration: Heating can decompose carbonates and nitrates. Green copper carbonate turns black and gives carbon dioxide. Zinc nitrate gives brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide, and a residue that is yellow when hot and white when cold. Potassium chlorate gives oxygen.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: heating copper carbonate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Green copper(II) carbonate is heated in a dry test tube. Write the balanced equation and state two observations.

**Step 1.** Products: black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide.

**Step 2.** Equation: $\ce{CuCO3 ->[\Delta] CuO + CO2}$ (Cu, C and O balance as they are).

**Step 3.** Observations: the green powder turns **black**, and the gas turns lime water **milky**.

visual.alt: Copper carbonate on heating gives copper oxide and carbon dioxide
visual.caption: One reactant, two products.

slides.narration: Heat splits copper carbonate into black copper oxide and carbon dioxide gas. Count the atoms: one copper, one carbon and three oxygen on each side, so the equation is already balanced. You see a colour change from green to black, and the gas turns lime water milky.

slides.heading: Decomposition by light
slides.body_md: Silver chloride and silver bromide split in **sunlight** to give silver and a halogen. This is why they are stored in dark bottles and used on photographic film.

visual.alt: Silver chloride in light gives silver and chlorine
visual.caption: White silver chloride turns grey as silver forms.

slides.narration: Some compounds are sensitive to light. White silver chloride turns grey in sunlight because tiny particles of silver form, and chlorine is given off. Silver bromide does the same, which is the basis of black and white photography.

slides.heading: Decomposition by electricity
slides.body_md: Passing a current through **acidified water** splits it into hydrogen at the **cathode** and oxygen at the **anode**, in the volume ratio **2 : 1**.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: heating zinc nitrate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Balance $\ce{Zn(NO3)2 -> ZnO + NO2 + O2}$ and state what is seen on heating.

**Step 1.** Oxygen is the awkward element, so try $2\ce{Zn(NO3)2}$ on the left: Zn 2, N 4, O 12.

**Step 2.** Right side: $2\ce{ZnO}$, $4\ce{NO2}$ and $\ce{O2}$: Zn 2, N 4, O $2 + 8 + 2 = 12$.

**Step 3.** Observations: brown fumes; the residue is yellow when hot and white when cold.

visual.alt: Two zinc nitrate give two zinc oxide, four nitrogen dioxide and one oxygen
visual.caption: Zn 2 = 2; N 4 = 4; O 12 = 12.

slides.narration: Start with zinc nitrate, which has two nitrate groups, and balance with two units. That gives two zinc, four nitrogen and twelve oxygen on the left. On the right, two zinc oxide, four nitrogen dioxide and one oxygen molecule also give twelve oxygen atoms. Brown fumes are seen.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Direct combination: two or more substances form one product (Fe + S → FeS).
Decomposition: one compound splits into simpler substances.
Heat: carbonates and nitrates; light: silver chloride and bromide; electricity: acidified water.
Always balance the equation and note the colour changes and gases.

visual.alt: Summary table of four reaction types and one example each

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. In combination, substances join. In decomposition, a compound splits, using heat, light or electricity. Examples are magnesium burning, copper carbonate heated, silver chloride in sunlight and water split by electricity.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Say what energy is used: heat, light or electricity.
Write colours with the substance: green copper carbonate turns black.
In electrolysis of water, hydrogen is twice the volume of oxygen.
Balance the equation and check each element.

rows: Calling heating copper carbonate a combination
Writing the water test gas as oxygen at the cathode
Write the condition above the arrow

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Name the form of energy. Give colours with the substances. Remember that hydrogen has twice the volume of oxygen in electrolysis. And balance every equation you write.

decks.title: Chemical Changes and Reactions — Part 2: Displacement, double decomposition and energy changes
goals: Predict whether a metal will displace another metal from its salt solution
Write balanced equations for the three prescribed double displacement reactions and state the colour of each precipitate
Classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic and give examples involving heat, light and electricity

slides.heading: Swapping partners
slides.body_md: Part 2 — in a **displacement** reaction one element pushes another out of a compound. In a **double displacement** two compounds exchange partners. Finally we ask where the energy goes.

visual.alt: Flow: A plus BC gives AC plus B in a displacement reaction

slides.narration: Some metals are more eager to react than others. A more reactive metal can push a less reactive metal out of its salt. We will use the order of reactivity to predict this, then look at reactions where two salts swap partners and form a precipitate.

slides.heading: The activity series
slides.body_md: A metal **higher** in the series displaces any metal **lower** than itself from a solution of its salt.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: zinc in copper sulphate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A piece of zinc is placed in blue copper(II) sulphate solution. Predict the reaction, write the equation and state the observations.

**Step 1.** Zinc is above copper in the series, so zinc **displaces** copper.

**Step 2.** $\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}$.

**Step 3.** The blue colour **fades** and a reddish-brown deposit of **copper** forms on the zinc.

visual.alt: Zinc plus copper sulphate gives zinc sulphate plus copper
visual.caption: Zinc is more reactive than copper.

slides.narration: Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it pushes copper out of the solution. The blue colour of the copper sulphate fades, because colourless zinc sulphate is forming, and reddish brown copper settles on the zinc.

slides.heading: Will it react?

visual.alt: Table predicting four displacement reactions from the activity series

slides.narration: Always compare positions. Iron is above copper, so it displaces copper. Copper is below zinc, so nothing happens. Zinc is above lead, so zinc pushes out lead. Silver is below copper, so there is no reaction.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: copper wire in silver nitrate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A coil of copper wire is hung in colourless silver nitrate solution. What is seen?

**Step 1.** Copper is above silver, so copper displaces silver.

**Step 2.** $\ce{Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag}$.

**Step 3.** Shiny grey **silver** crystals grow on the wire and the solution turns **blue**.

visual.alt: Copper plus two silver nitrate gives copper nitrate plus two silver
visual.caption: Two silver atoms are displaced.

slides.narration: Copper is above silver, so it displaces silver. Shiny silver crystals form on the copper wire. The solution slowly turns blue, because copper nitrate is blue.

slides.heading: Double displacement and precipitates
slides.body_md: In **double displacement** (double decomposition) the positive parts of two compounds **exchange** partners: $\ce{AB + CD -> AD + CB}$. One product is often an insoluble solid, a **precipitate**.

nodes.label: New pairs A⁺ D⁻ and C⁺ B⁻

visual.alt: Flow showing two solutions exchanging partners to give a precipitate

slides.narration: Two solutions are mixed. The positive and negative parts swap partners. If one of the new pairs does not dissolve, it appears as solid particles, called a precipitate, and the liquid turns cloudy.

visual.alt: Table of the three double displacement reactions and the colours of the precipitates

sections.heading: 1. Direct combination reactions
sections.body_md:
In a **direct combination** reaction two or more substances (elements or compounds) unite to form **one** product.

| Reactants | Equation | Condition and observation |
|---|---|---|
| Iron + sulphur | $\ce{Fe + S -> FeS}$ | Heat; red glow; black iron(II) sulphide, not attracted by a magnet |
| Magnesium + oxygen | $\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}$ | Heat; dazzling white flame; white ash |
| Carbon + oxygen | $\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}$ | Heat; colourless gas that turns lime water milky |
| Hydrogen + chlorine | $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$ | Sunlight (or burning in chlorine); hydrogen chloride gas |
| Nitrogen + oxygen | $\ce{N2 + O2 -> 2NO}$ | Electric spark or very high temperature |
| Quicklime + water | $\ce{CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2}$ | Hissing; much heat; slaked lime |
| Ammonia + hydrogen chloride | $\ce{NH3 + HCl -> NH4Cl}$ | Dense white fumes of ammonium chloride |

The product is a compound in each case; combinations of elements are also called **synthesis**. A mixture of iron and sulphur can be separated with a magnet, but iron(II) sulphide cannot.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which two or more substances unite to form a single product.

sections.heading: 2. Decomposition by heat, light and electricity
sections.body_md:
In a **decomposition** reaction one compound splits into two or more simpler substances. It needs energy.

**Thermal decomposition (heat)**

| Substance | Equation | What is seen |
|---|---|---|
| Copper(II) carbonate | $\ce{CuCO3 ->[\Delta] CuO + CO2}$ | Green powder turns black; gas turns lime water milky |
| Zinc carbonate | $\ce{ZnCO3 ->[\Delta] ZnO + CO2}$ | Residue yellow when hot, white when cold |
| Calcium carbonate | $\ce{CaCO3 ->[\Delta] CaO + CO2}$ | White solid; needs strong heating |
| Zinc nitrate | $\ce{2Zn(NO3)2 ->[\Delta] 2ZnO + 4NO2 + O2}$ | Brown fumes; residue yellow hot, white cold |
| Lead(II) nitrate | $\ce{2Pb(NO3)2 ->[\Delta] 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2}$ | Crackling; brown fumes; yellow residue |
| Potassium chlorate | $\ce{2KClO3 ->[\Delta] 2KCl + 3O2}$ | Oxygen (relights a glowing splint); manganese dioxide speeds it |
| Ammonium chloride | $\ce{NH4Cl ->[\Delta] NH3 + HCl}$ | White solid disappears and re-forms on the cool part of the tube |

**Photo decomposition (light):** $\ce{2AgCl ->[light] 2Ag + Cl2}$; white silver chloride turns grey. Silver bromide behaves in the same way ($\ce{2AgBr ->[light] 2Ag + Br2}$), so these salts are kept in dark bottles and are used in photographic film.

**Electrolytic decomposition (electricity):** $\ce{2H2O ->[electricity] 2H2 + O2}$ for acidified water: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode in the volume ratio 2 : 1. Molten lead(II) bromide gives lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode.

Mercury(II) oxide breaks down into mercury and oxygen on heating, but mercury is toxic, so it is not done in school laboratories.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction in which one compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances.
Decomposition of a compound by passing an electric current through it in the molten or dissolved state.

sections.heading: 3. Displacement reactions and reactivity
sections.body_md:
In a **displacement** reaction a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound. For metals the order of reactivity is the **activity series**:

K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Hg, Ag, Au (most to least reactive).

A metal displaces any metal **below** it from a solution of its salt, and not one above it.

| Metal | Salt solution | Equation and observation |
|---|---|---|
| Zinc | Copper(II) sulphate | $\ce{Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu}$; blue colour fades; reddish-brown copper |
| Iron | Copper(II) sulphate | $\ce{Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu}$; blue changes to pale green; copper on the nail |
| Copper | Silver nitrate | $\ce{Cu + 2AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2Ag}$; silver crystals; solution turns blue |
| Magnesium | Iron(II) sulphate | $\ce{Mg + FeSO4 -> MgSO4 + Fe}$; pale green fades |
| Copper | Zinc sulphate | No reaction: copper is below zinc |

The more reactive metal goes into solution as its ion; the less reactive metal is deposited. Reactive metals such as sodium and potassium react with water, so they are not used in salt-solution displacement.

The list of metals in order of their reactivity, from most to least reactive.

sections.heading: 4. Double decomposition (double displacement)
sections.body_md:
In **double decomposition** two compounds, usually in solution, exchange their positive and negative parts: AB + CD → AD + CB. When one product is **insoluble**, it settles as a **precipitate**.

| Mix | Equation | Precipitate and colour |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium sulphate + barium chloride | $\ce{Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 v + 2NaCl}$ | Barium sulphate: **white** |
| Silver nitrate + sodium chloride | $\ce{AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl v + NaNO3}$ | Silver chloride: **white, curdy**; turns grey in light |
| Lead nitrate + potassium iodide | $\ce{Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 v + 2KNO3}$ | Lead iodide: **yellow** |

The colour of the precipitate helps to identify the ions: a white precipitate with barium chloride shows sulphate, a white curdy one with silver nitrate shows chloride and a yellow one with lead nitrate shows iodide. Books describe the lead iodide precipitate as bright yellow and the barium sulphate as fine white; both are insoluble in water.

A reaction in which two compounds exchange their positive and negative parts.

sections.heading: 5. Energy changes in reactions
sections.body_md:
Every chemical change involves a change of energy.

- An **exothermic** reaction **gives out** energy (heat, light or electricity) to the surroundings: the temperature of the mixture rises.
- An **endothermic** reaction **takes in** energy from the surroundings: the temperature falls, or energy must be supplied.

| Energy | Evolved (exothermic) | Absorbed (endothermic) |
|---|---|---|
| Heat | Burning of carbon and fuels; quicklime with water; acid with alkali (neutralisation); respiration | Heating calcium carbonate; $\ce{N2 + O2 -> 2NO}$ at a high temperature |
| Light | Burning magnesium (dazzling white light) | Photosynthesis; silver chloride and bromide in sunlight |
| Electricity | A cell, such as a dry cell or a zinc and copper cell | Electrolysis of water or molten lead(II) bromide |

Photosynthesis: $\ce{6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2}$ takes in light; respiration: $\ce{C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O}$ gives out energy. Baking soda with citric acid is a safe endothermic reaction: the cup turns cold.

key_terms.definition_md: A reaction that gives out energy (as heat, light or electricity) to the surroundings.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Not saying which form of energy (heat, light or electricity) causes a decomposition.
- Writing the precipitate colour wrongly: silver chloride is white and curdy, not yellow; lead iodide is yellow.
- Predicting that a metal displaces one that is higher in the series.
- Forgetting the 2 in 2NaCl, 2KI or 2AgNO₃ when balancing.
- Writing hydrogen at the anode in the electrolysis of acidified water (it is at the cathode).
- Calling a reaction exothermic because it needs heating to start; look at the net energy change.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a balanced equation, a colour, an observation or a name.
- 2 marks: an equation with one observation, or a prediction with its reason.
- 3 marks: three equations or three observations; a labelled diagram.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation or an experiment with parts of 2 to 4 marks; balanced equations, observations and a diagram.

(b) Name the gases collected in tubes A and B and give a test for each. [3]

(c) Why is a little acid added to the water? [1]

(d) Write the balanced equation for the decomposition of water. [1]

(e) If 24 cm³ of gas is collected in tube A, what volume of gas is collected in tube B at the same time? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **C** is the **acidified water**; **D** is the **cathode** (negative electrode); **E** is the **battery**.

**(b)** **A** holds **hydrogen**, which burns with a **pop** near a flame. **B** holds **oxygen**, which **relights a glowing splint**.

**(c)** Pure water is a poor conductor; the acid supplies **ions** so that the current can pass.

**(d)** $\ce{2H2O ->[electricity] 2H2 + O2}$

**(e)** Hydrogen is twice the volume of oxygen, so tube B holds **12 cm³** (24 ÷ 2).

A student places strips of zinc, iron and copper in solutions of zinc sulphate, iron(II) sulphate and copper(II) sulphate. A tick shows that a reaction occurred and a cross shows no reaction.

| Metal | Zinc sulphate | Iron(II) sulphate | Copper(II) sulphate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zinc | not used | ✓ | ✓ |
| Iron | ✗ | not used | ✓ |
| Copper | ✗ | ✗ | not used |

(a) Arrange the three metals in decreasing order of reactivity, with a reason. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equation for iron with copper(II) sulphate and state one observation. [3]

(c) Predict, with a reason, whether silver would displace copper from copper(II) sulphate solution. [2]

(d) Write the balanced equation for zinc with iron(II) sulphate solution and name the metal deposited. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Zinc > iron > copper.** Zinc displaces both others, iron displaces only copper, and copper displaces neither.

**(b)** $\ce{Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu}$; the **blue solution turns pale green** and **reddish-brown copper** is deposited on the iron.

**(c)** **No**, because silver is **below copper** in the activity series.

**(d)** $\ce{Zn + FeSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Fe}$; **iron** is deposited.

questions.solution_md: Zn > Fe > Cu; Fe + CuSO₄ with colour change; silver does not displace copper; Zn + FeSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Fe.

questions.stem_md:
Test tubes A, B and C hold the precipitates formed when the following pairs of solutions are mixed, in some order: sodium sulphate with barium chloride; silver nitrate with sodium chloride; lead nitrate with potassium iodide. The precipitate in tube C is yellow. The precipitate in tube B is curdy and turns grey when left in sunlight. The precipitate in tube A is a fine white powder.

(a) Identify the pair of solutions used and the precipitate formed in each tube. [3]

(b) Write the balanced equation for the reaction in tube C. [2]

(c) Write the balanced equation for the reaction in tube A. [2]

(d) Name the type of these three reactions. [1]

(e) Explain why the precipitate in tube B turns grey in sunlight. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A**: sodium sulphate with barium chloride, giving **barium sulphate**. **B**: silver nitrate with sodium chloride, giving **silver chloride**. **C**: lead nitrate with potassium iodide, giving **lead iodide**.

**(b)** $\ce{Pb(NO3)2 + 2KI -> PbI2 + 2KNO3}$

**(c)** $\ce{Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl}$

**(d)** **Double decomposition** (double displacement).

**(e)** Silver chloride is **decomposed by light** to **silver**, which is grey (with chlorine given off).

questions.solution_md: A BaSO₄; B AgCl; C PbI₂; two equations; double decomposition; light splits AgCl to silver.

questions.stem_md:
Three reactions are carried out in a polystyrene cup, each with 50 cm³ of liquid. Reaction P: quicklime is stirred into water (28 °C to 55 °C). Reaction Q: dilute hydrochloric acid is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution (27 °C to 33 °C). Reaction R: baking soda is stirred into citric acid solution (28 °C to 22 °C).

(a) Classify P, Q and R as exothermic or endothermic and give a reason for each. [3]

(b) Write the balanced equation for reaction P. [1]

(c) Give one example each of a reaction that evolves light and a reaction that evolves electricity. [2]

(d) Write a balanced equation for one reaction that absorbs light and one that absorbs electricity. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **P** is **exothermic** (temperature rises by 27 °C). **Q** is **exothermic** (rises by 6 °C). **R** is **endothermic** (falls by 6 °C): heat is taken from the liquid.

**(b)** $\ce{CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2}$

**(c)** **Light:** magnesium burning in air. **Electricity:** a dry cell (or a zinc and copper cell).

**(d)** **Light absorbed:** $\ce{6CO2 + 6H2O ->[light] C6H12O6 + 6O2}$ (photosynthesis). **Electricity absorbed:** $\ce{2H2O ->[electricity] 2H2 + O2}$.

questions.solution_md: P and Q exothermic, R endothermic; slaked lime; magnesium and a cell; photosynthesis and electrolysis.

questions.stem_md:
A teacher demonstrates three decompositions: (i) green copper(II) carbonate is heated in a dry test tube; (ii) white silver chloride is left in sunlight; (iii) molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed.

(a) Write a balanced equation for each reaction. [3]

(b) State one observation for each reaction. [3]

(c) Name the form of energy that causes each decomposition. [2]

(d) Name the substance formed at the cathode and at the anode in (iii). [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (i) $\ce{CuCO3 ->[\Delta] CuO + CO2}$

(ii) $\ce{2AgCl ->[light] 2Ag + Cl2}$

(iii) $\ce{PbBr2 ->[electricity] Pb + Br2}$

**(b)** (i) the green powder turns **black**; (ii) the white solid turns **grey**; (iii) a **silvery-grey bead of lead** forms and **reddish-brown fumes** of bromine appear.

**(c)** (i) **heat**; (ii) **light**; (iii) **electricity**.

**(d)** **Lead** at the cathode and **bromine** at the anode.

questions.solution_md: Three equations; green to black, white to grey, lead and bromine; heat, light, electricity; lead and bromine.
